phases.label: Define
phases.title: End-Goal Planning & Subsystem Scoping
phases.description: We open every season by breaking the game down before touching hardware. The Game Points Matrix maps every mission by risk, reward, and time cost — forcing honest prioritization before any design commitment. From this, we define robot capability targets per subsystem, setting measurable requirements that guide every decision downstream.
bullets: Game Points Matrix: score and rank every scoring mission
Monte Carlo simulation to predict score ranges and mission times
Subsystem capability targets set before prototyping begins
User and subsystem requirements documented in the DHF

phases.label: Hypothesize
phases.title: Advanced CAD Pre-Planning & Rough Prototypes
phases.description: With requirements locked, the team moves into 100% CAD-first design using Onshape. Every subsystem is modeled before a single physical part is made. Joints define motion ranges, assemblies validate clearances, and CAD-derived drawings feed directly into CNC toolpaths. Rough prototypes test risky mechanisms early, when changes are cheap.
bullets: Full robot modeled in Onshape — no part fabricated before CAD review
Subsystems designed with joints to define and validate motion ranges
FMEA (Failure Mode Effect Analysis) to catch failure modes before build
Rough physical prototypes validate high-risk subsystem assumptions

phases.label: Fabricate
phases.title: Finalize Designs & Advanced Fabrication
phases.description: Finalized CAD drives production. 3D printing handles complex geometry; CNC milling produces structural aluminum, acrylic, and plate components. Because the robot is 100% CAD-designed, CNC setup is straightforward — every part traces back to a model. Integration testing runs against the requirements defined in Phase 1.
bullets: 3D printing for complex geometry and custom mechanism parts
CNC milling for structural aluminum, plate work, and precision components
Performance testing against Phase 1 requirements; DHF updated with results
